Guided Inquiry

Two stars, one blob

Two point sources sit 2 mm apart, 10 m away. Through a 2 mm circular aperture at 550 nm they look like one fuzzy blob (see the scene). What would actually let you tell them apart?

Try it: widen the aperture

Drag the aperture slider up. The two stars stay exactly where they are; each Airy disc shrinks, and a valley opens between the two peaks in the profile below.

The Rayleigh limit is not the moment the valley first appears — a shallow one appears earlier. It is the moment the valley floor reaches 73.5% of the peak, marked by the dashed green line: there the peak of one disc sits on the first dark ring of the other.

What if the light were bluer?

Set aperture back to 2 mm. The pair is unresolved. Now predict: what happens to the minimum resolvable separation if you switch from 550 nm (green) to 400 nm (violet)?

Full simulation

All three sliders are live: aperture D, star separation s, and wavelength λ. The top panel is what the observer sees; the graph below is the combined brightness across that image. The sidebar reports θmin = 1.22 λ/D and the smallest gap it can resolve at 10 m.

Rule of thumb: resolved ⇔ actual gap ≥ smallest resolvable gap. Doubling D halves the limit; shorter λ lowers it too. Magnification appears nowhere in θmin = 1.22 λ/D — which is why it cannot help.

verdict—
The pair counts as resolved once the actual gap reaches the smallest resolvable one. That is Rayleigh's criterion — an agreed convention, not a sudden physical change: at exactly that gap the peak of one Airy disc (the bright blob a round aperture makes of a point source) sits on the first dark ring of the other, and the valley between them is at 73.5% of the peak.

01

At a glance

Two stars that are close together can look like one blob. This sim puts two point sources 10 m away, views them through a circular opening, and shows both the image the observer sees and how the brightness varies across it.

What you'll learn

  • Why a point source never forms a point image.
  • What it means for two sources to be resolved, and how the brightness profile shows it.
  • Which quantities decide whether a close pair is seen as two.
The apparatus. Two point stars a distance s apart, seen through a circular opening of diameter D. The angle α is between the two directions.

What's on screen

  • Star A: the warm one. Its pattern is drawn with a dashed marker in the lower graph.
  • Star B: the cool one, marked with a dotted line.
  • Upper panel: what the observer sees. Lower panel: the combined brightness across that image.

The aperture and the verdict are written in the badge at the bottom left of the upper panel. The distance is fixed at 10 m.

See itUse the opening setup, D = 2.0 mm, s = 2.00 mm and λ = 550 nm. Watch for: two labelled stars in the upper panel, a graph of brightness below it, and a verdict in the badge.

03

Each star arrives as a disc, not a point

A star is a point source, but light that passes through a round opening is diffracted. The image of one star is a bright central disc surrounded by faint rings, called the Airy pattern.

The two stars are unrelated, so their light does not interfere. Their brightnesses simply add. Each star's pattern is centred on its own direction, and the two directions differ by the angle α = s/L.

  • At the opening values, α = 2.00 mm / 10 m = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ rad.
  • The lower graph adds the two patterns along the line through the stars. One hump looks like one blob.
  • Two humps with a dip between them look like two stars. The pair is resolved when the dip is clear enough.
See itLook at the two stars at the opening setup. Watch for: two overlapping glowing discs ringed by faint rings, and a single hump in the graph below.
04

The first dark ring lies at 1.22 λ/D, so a wider aperture makes a smaller disc

The brightness follows I ∝ [2J₁(u)/u]², with u = πD sin θ / λ. The first zero of the Bessel function J₁ is at u = 3.832, and 3.832/π = 1.22. That is where the first dark ring sits, so the disc has angular radius:

θmin = 1.22 λ/D
For a circular aperture of diameter D.
  • Doubling D halves the disc. The stars do not move, so the discs shrink away from each other.
  • At the opening values θmin = 1.22 × 550 nm / 2.0 mm = 3.36 × 10⁻⁴ rad. At 10 m that spans 3.355 mm, more than the 2.00 mm gap, so the discs overlap.
  • A slit uses 1 instead of 1.22, so a circle needs 22% more angle.
See itDouble the aperture to D = 4.0 mm. Watch for: smallest resolvable angle 1.68e−4 rad in the readouts, much smaller discs, and a dip between two humps in the graph.
05

Two stars are resolved when the gap reaches the Rayleigh limit

Rayleigh's criterion is an agreed convention. The pair counts as resolved when the peak of one disc sits on the first dark ring of the other, so the angle between the stars is at least θmin. At distance L that gap is:

smin = L tan θmin ≈ 1.22 λL/D
Resolved when s ≥ smin.
  • At the opening values smin = 3.355 mm. The actual gap is 2.00 mm, which is 0.60 of that, so the verdict is unresolved.
  • At exactly the limit the valley between the peaks is at 73.5% of the peak. The sim draws that level as a dashed line.
  • A shallow dip appears earlier, from about 0.78 of smin. The limit is a convention, not the first moment a dip appears.
See itSet D = 3.4 mm, just past the limit. Watch for: smallest resolvable gap 1.974 mm, a valley floor at 71% of the peak just under the dashed 73.5% line, and a verdict of RESOLVED.
06

Magnifying the image cannot split the pair

Magnification scales the whole picture. The discs grow, and the gap between the stars grows by the same factor. The overlap, the ratio s/smin and the depth of the valley are all unchanged. A bigger version of one blob is still one blob.

  • θmin = 1.22 λ/D contains no magnification. Only the aperture and the wavelength appear.
  • The detail was lost when the light passed through the opening. An eyepiece works on the light that is already there.
  • That is why a larger telescope mirror, not a stronger eyepiece, separates a close double star.

The sim has no magnification control, so none of the sliders can mimic it. Only D, s and λ change the verdict.

07

A shorter wavelength resolves a smaller gap

θmin = 1.22 λ/D is proportional to λ, so the smallest resolvable gap shrinks with the wavelength. Bluer light gives finer detail through the same aperture.

  • At D = 2.0 mm, smin is 2.318 mm at 380 nm, 3.355 mm at 550 nm and 4.270 mm at 700 nm.
  • At 400 nm it is 2.44 mm. That is lower than 3.36 mm, but still more than the 2.00 mm gap, so the pair stays unresolved.
  • To resolve this pair at D = 2.0 mm the wavelength would need to be below about 328 nm, which is ultraviolet and off the slider.

The same idea explains why microscopes that use ultraviolet light or electron beams see finer detail.

See itSwitch to blue light, λ = 400 nm. Watch for: smallest resolvable gap 2.440 mm in the readouts, a smaller disc, and a verdict that is still unresolved.
08

The gap, aperture and wavelength together set the verdict

The verdict compares the actual gap s with smin = 1.22 λL/D. Moving the stars apart is as good as widening the aperture.

  • At D = 2.0 mm and 550 nm, s = 3.35 mm is still unresolved and s = 3.40 mm is resolved, because smin = 3.355 mm.
  • For a pair 0.50 mm apart, D must be at least 13.42 mm. On the slider, 13.4 mm fails and 13.5 mm passes.
  • The tightest pair, s = 0.2 mm, is never resolved on these sliders. The best case, D = 20 mm at 380 nm, gives smin = 0.232 mm.
See itKeep D = 2.0 mm and move the stars apart to s = 3.40 mm. Watch for: their actual gap s 3.40 mm against 3.355 mm, a dip between two humps, and a verdict of RESOLVED.
09

Summary

In one line. A round opening smears each point source into a disc, and the combined brightness of the two discs shows whether the stars are told apart.

Key points

  • θmin = 1.22 λ/D, and smin = L tan θmin ≈ 1.22 λL/D.
  • The pair is resolved when s ≥ smin. At the limit the valley is at 73.5% of the peak.
  • A wider aperture or a shorter wavelength lowers the limit. Magnification does not.

Common mix-ups

  • "I need more magnification." A bigger blob is still one blob. Widen the aperture instead.
  • "Resolved means a dip just appeared." A shallow dip comes earlier. The criterion is a convention.

Things to try on your own

  • Set D = 20 mm and λ = 380 nm, and read the smallest gap. It is 0.232 mm.
  • Set s = 8.00 mm and find the smallest D that resolves it. It is 0.9 mm.
